unit.title: Implement and maintain internal control procedures

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the main purpose of internal control in an organisation?
options: To guarantee that no fraud or error can ever occur
To give reasonable assurance that aims are met
To replace the need for an external audit
To send every decision to the board

questions.stem: Which set best describes what internal controls aim to protect or achieve?
options: Assets, reliable records, compliance and efficiency
Market share, brand image and staff morale
Sales growth, pricing and new product ideas
Share price, dividends and lower tax bills

questions.stem: The finance director of a Kingston distributor often overrides procedures to 'get things done', and staff copy him. Which part of the internal control system is weakest?

The year-end stock count
The payroll software
The control environment

questions.stem: A manager is setting up controls for a new online sales process. What should she do first?

questions.stem: Risks are scored as likelihood × impact, each on a scale of 1 to 5. Risk A: likelihood 4, impact 3. Risk B: likelihood 2, impact 5. Risk C: likelihood 5, impact 2. Risk D: likelihood 3, impact 3. Which has the highest score?
options: Risk A

questions.stem: Which control best prevents false credit notes being issued to customers?

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What term names the check of the purchase order, goods received note and supplier invoice against each other before payment?
What one-word term describes a control, such as an approval, that is designed to stop an error or fraud before it happens?
What one-word term describes a control, such as restoring data from a back-up, that puts things right after a problem is found?
A supplier's statement shows a balance of J$1,276,500. The firm's ledger shows J$1,198,000 for that supplier. What is the difference to be explained, in J$?
What one-word term names the regular comparison of two sets of records, such as the ledger and a supplier statement, to find and explain differences?
What two-word term names a rule that staff in sensitive finance roles must take their leave, so that others cover their work?
What one-word term names a person who reports suspected wrongdoing in an organisation through a protected channel?
What two-word term names a control that makes up for a weakness elsewhere, such as an owner's review where duties cannot be separated?
A cashier starts with a float of J$15,000. The till records takings of J$186,400. The cash counted at closing is J$199,900. What is the cash shortage, in J$?
What two-word term names the record in a computer system that shows who made each change or entry, and when?
What one-word term names a test in which a manager follows one transaction through a process from start to finish to see that each control works?
What two-word term names a table showing each role's spending and approval limits?
What two-word term names an unannounced count of cash or stock, made to check that it agrees with the records?
Stock records show 1,250 units, but a count finds 1,190. What percentage of the recorded stock is missing?
What one-word term names the ongoing checking that controls are still working as intended?

essays.stem: Explain the purpose and the main parts of an internal control system, using examples from a medium-sized wholesale business.
essays.modelAnswer: Internal control is the set of policies, procedures and checks that give management reasonable assurance that assets are protected, records are reliable, laws are followed and work is done efficiently. It cannot remove all risk, but it reduces errors and fraud to an acceptable level. The first part is the control environment: the attitude of the owners and managers, shown in a code of conduct, clear roles and their own respect for procedures. The second is risk assessment: in a wholesaler, the main risks include stock theft, payments to false suppliers and errors in customer credit. The third is control activities, such as approval limits for purchases, separating ordering, receiving and paying, three-way matching, stock counts and restricted system access. The fourth is information and communication: written procedures, accurate reports and clear lines for reporting problems. The fifth is monitoring: managers review exception reports, test samples of transactions, and internal audit reports weaknesses to management and the audit committee. All five must work together; strong checks are of little use if managers routinely override them.
markingPoints: Purpose: reasonable assurance over assets, records, compliance and efficiency
Control environment with an example
Risk assessment and control activities with wholesale examples
Information and communication
Monitoring, and how the parts work together

essays.stem: Describe the controls you would put in place over the purchase-to-payment process of a distribution company in Spanish Town.
essays.modelAnswer: I would begin with an approved supplier list, with new suppliers checked and approved by someone outside the buying team, and supplier bank details changed only after confirming the request by phone on a number already on file. Purchases would start with a requisition and a numbered purchase order approved within the limits in the authorisation matrix. Goods would be received by the stores, who would check them against the order and complete a goods received note. Accounts payable would match the order, the goods received note and the invoice before entering it, and query any differences in price or quantity. Ordering, receiving, recording and paying would be done by different people. Payments would be prepared from approved invoices only and released by two authorised signatories, with the system blocking payments to suppliers not on the list. Each month, supplier statements would be reconciled to the ledger and an exception report of large payments and master file changes reviewed by the finance manager. These controls would be written up, staff trained, and samples tested every quarter.
markingPoints: Approved supplier list and verified bank detail changes
Numbered, approved purchase orders within limits
Goods received checks and three-way matching
Separation of duties and dual payment release
Monthly reconciliations, exception reports and testing

essays.stem: A manager scores three risks on likelihood and impact, each from 1 to 5. Risk A, payments to fake supplier accounts: likelihood 3, impact 5. Risk B, theft of stock from the warehouse: likelihood 4, impact 3. Risk C, errors in sales invoices: likelihood 4, impact 2. Calculate each score, rank the risks, and recommend a control for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Multiplying likelihood by impact gives: Risk A, 3 × 5 = 15; Risk B, 4 × 3 = 12; Risk C, 4 × 2 = 8. The ranking is therefore A first, then B, then C. Risk A should be dealt with first because a single fake payment could be very large and may not be recovered. The main control is that supplier bank details can be changed only by an officer outside accounts payable, after the request is confirmed by phone using contact details already on file, and a weekly exception report of all changes is reviewed by the finance manager. For Risk B, the warehouse should be locked with access limited to stores staff, every movement recorded, and regular surprise counts made by staff independent of the stores, with differences investigated. For Risk C, which is less serious, invoices should be produced from approved price lists in the system, with a sample checked each week by a supervisor and customer queries tracked. Each control should have a named owner and be tested, and the scores reviewed after the controls are in place.
markingPoints: Scores calculated correctly: 15, 12 and 8
Ranked A, B, C with reasons
Suitable control for supplier payment fraud
Suitable controls for stock theft and invoice errors
Owners, testing and re-scoring

essays.stem: Describe the internal controls a public agency with 300 staff should have over its payroll.
essays.modelAnswer: Only the human resources unit should be able to add new staff or change pay rates, and only on signed, approved documents such as appointment letters. Payroll staff should process pay but should not be able to create employees, so the duties are separated. Every change to the payroll, such as starters, leavers, promotions and deductions, should appear on a change report that a senior officer checks against the source documents before each pay run. Hours, overtime and allowances should be approved by line managers before they are paid. Each pay run should be compared with the previous one, and large differences explained. Pay should go by bank transfer to accounts in the employee's own name, with any change of bank details confirmed with the employee directly. From time to time, the agency should check that every person paid is a real employee in post, for example by a headcount or by managers confirming their staff lists. Access to the payroll system should be by unique log-in, with an audit trail. Internal audit should test payroll controls regularly.
markingPoints: HR authorises starters, leavers and pay changes
Separation between HR and payroll processing
Change reports and pay-run comparisons checked by a senior officer
Approved hours and verified bank details
Headcount checks, system access controls and audit testing

essays.stem: Describe how you would test whether the controls over supplier payments are working, and what you would do with the results.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by reading the written procedure and listing the key controls, such as approval within limits, three-way matching, two signatories and checks on bank detail changes. I would do a walkthrough, following one payment from order to bank transfer, to confirm the controls exist in practice. Then I would choose a sample of payments from the period, for example 40, picked at random and including some large ones. For each, I would check the evidence: the approved order, the goods received note, the matched invoice, the correct approver and both release signatures. I would also check a sample of supplier master file changes for independent confirmation. I would record each test in a spreadsheet and note every exception, then calculate the exception rate for each control. Where I found exceptions, I would find the cause, such as unclear limits or missing training. I would report the results to the finance manager and, for significant weaknesses, to the audit committee, with recommended actions, owners and dates. I would then follow up to make sure the actions were completed and retest the controls.
markingPoints: Identifies key controls and performs a walkthrough
Selects a suitable sample
Checks evidence for each control and records exceptions
Calculates rates and finds causes
Reports, agrees actions and follows up with retesting

essays.stem: Evaluate the controls needed over a cloud-based accounting system used by a growing Kingston firm.
essays.modelAnswer: Cloud accounting brings benefits, such as access from anywhere, automatic updates and back-ups by the provider, but it also creates risks: unauthorised access, data loss, and errors spreading quickly through linked processes. Access control is the most important area. Each user should have a unique log-in with strong passwords and two-step sign-in, and rights should match the user's role, so that, for example, the person entering invoices cannot approve payments or change supplier details. Access should be removed promptly when staff leave and reviewed every quarter. The audit trail should be switched on and reviewed for unusual changes. Automated controls, such as payment limits, required fields and duplicate invoice checks, should be set up and tested before use. The firm should confirm the provider's security and back-up arrangements in the contract, make sure data is handled in line with the data protection law, and keep its own regular export of key data. Changes to settings should be approved and recorded. Overall, cloud systems can be well controlled, but only if the firm actively manages access and settings rather than leaving them to the provider.
markingPoints: Weighs benefits against risks
Role-based access, strong log-in and prompt removal
Audit trail review and tested automated controls
Provider contract, back-ups and data protection
Change control and a reasoned overall judgement

essays.stem: Using the fraud triangle, explain why fraud happens in organisations and how internal controls and culture can reduce it.
essays.modelAnswer: The fraud triangle says that fraud usually needs three conditions. Pressure is a personal or work need, such as debt, illness in the family or unrealistic targets. Opportunity is a weakness that lets the person commit and hide the fraud, such as one person controlling a whole process. Rationalisation is the way the person justifies it, such as 'I am underpaid' or 'I will pay it back'. Internal controls act mainly on opportunity. Separating duties, approvals, reconciliations, restricted system access, surprise counts and mandatory leave all make fraud harder to commit and more likely to be found. The belief that fraud will be detected is itself a strong deterrent. Culture acts on pressure and rationalisation. Managers who set realistic targets, treat staff fairly and offer support, such as an employee assistance programme, reduce pressure. A clear code of conduct, managers who follow the rules themselves, prompt and fair action when fraud is found, and a safe whistleblowing channel make it harder for people to justify dishonesty. Controls and culture work best together.
markingPoints: Explains pressure with examples
Explains opportunity and rationalisation
Controls reduce opportunity and raise detection
Culture reduces pressure and rationalisation
Concludes that both are needed

essays.stem: Evaluate the costs and benefits of internal controls, and explain how a manager decides how much control is enough.
essays.modelAnswer: Controls bring clear benefits. They protect cash and other assets, reduce errors, make reports reliable for decisions, help the organisation meet the law and give confidence to owners, lenders and auditors. They also deter fraud. However, controls have costs. Some are direct, such as staff time, software and audit fees. Others are hidden: extra approvals slow down purchasing and customer service, and too many checks can frustrate staff and make them look for ways round the rules. A manager decides how much control is enough by starting with a risk assessment. For each process, she considers how likely a problem is and how much harm it would cause, and then compares the cost of a control with the expected loss it prevents. High risks, such as payments and payroll, justify strong controls even if they are costly. Low risks, such as small stationery purchases, may need only simple controls or none. She should prefer controls built into normal work and systems, review them as risks change, and remove controls that no longer add value.
markingPoints: Benefits of controls
Direct and hidden costs, including delay and frustration
Uses risk assessment to set the level of control
Compares control cost with expected loss
Reviews and removes controls that add no value

essays.stem: An internal audit report on your department lists three control weaknesses: no review of supplier bank detail changes, stock counts done by the storekeeper alone, and shared system passwords. Describe how you would respond.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first meet the internal auditor to make sure I understand each finding, its evidence and its risk, and I would brief my manager. I would treat the unchecked bank detail changes as the most urgent, because it could lead to large, unrecoverable payments. I would immediately check recent changes against confirmations from the suppliers and introduce independent approval of all changes, with a weekly exception report. For the stock counts, I would arrange for counts to be done by staff from outside the stores, with the storekeeper present but not counting, and for differences to be investigated and approved. For the shared passwords, I would work with IT to give each user a unique log-in, set access rights by role and switch on the audit trail. I would then write a management response with the action, owner and completion date for each finding, and update the procedures manual and train staff. I would track progress in a simple action log, report it at each audit committee meeting, and ask internal audit to retest once the changes are in place.
markingPoints: Understands the findings and briefs management
Prioritises by risk and takes urgent action on the highest risk
Practical fix for each of the three weaknesses
Management response with owners and dates, procedures and training
Tracks progress, reports and requests retesting

essays.stem: Justify why the 'tone at the top' is critical to internal control, and recommend how a new chief executive of a Montego Bay hotel group can strengthen it.
essays.modelAnswer: The tone at the top is the attitude of the board and senior managers towards honesty, rules and control. It is critical because staff copy what leaders do, not just what they say. If senior managers override procedures, approve their own expenses or ignore warnings, staff conclude that controls do not matter, and even well-designed checks fail. Most serious frauds involve someone senior or a weak culture that let problems go unchallenged. A strong tone makes controls part of normal work and encourages people to report concerns. The new chief executive should first set out clear expectations in a code of conduct and speak about them openly. She should follow the rules herself, for example by having her own expenses approved by the chair. She should make sure the board or audit committee receives regular reports on control weaknesses and fraud, and that internal audit is independent. She should support a confidential whistleblowing channel and protect those who use it. When breaches occur, she should act consistently, whatever the person's level. Finally, she should recognise managers who run their areas with sound controls.
markingPoints: Defines tone at the top
Explains why staff behaviour follows leaders and how controls fail otherwise
Leader models the rules and sets a code of conduct
Oversight by board or audit committee and independent internal audit
Whistleblowing, consistent action and recognition

practical1.title: Map a purchasing process and build a risk and control matrix
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack describing how a made-up organisation (for example a Spanish Town distribution firm or a municipal corporation office) buys goods and pays suppliers, with interview notes, sample documents and a list of recent problems. As a group, produce: a flowchart of the current process from request to payment, showing who does each step; a risk and control matrix in a spreadsheet, listing at least eight risks, each scored for likelihood and impact (1 to 5), the existing control, any gap and the recommended control; a revised two-page procedure that closes the main gaps; and a one-page memo to the finance manager summarising the changes and how staff will be trained. Give each member a named role: team lead (keeps time and writes the memo), process mapper (draws the flowchart), risk analyst (scores the risks), controls designer (recommends controls), and procedure writer (writes the revised procedure). In a group of four, the team lead also writes the procedure. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Case pack from the assessor, including interview notes and sample documents
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
photos: The draft flowchart on the flipchart, built with sticky notes
The finished flowchart showing who does each step
The risk and control matrix on screen, with scores
The memo to the finance manager
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Flowchart shows the real process and who does each step
Risks are relevant and scored correctly
Recommended controls address the gaps and separate duties where possible
Procedure is clear, practical and matches the matrix
Considered cost and practicality, not just adding approvals
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up case and invented names
Keep the case pack and outputs confidential to the group and the assessor
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Test a payment control, report the results and agree actions
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group copies of 40 made-up payment files for a public agency or a hotel group: each has a purchase order, goods received note, invoice and payment voucher, and some contain errors or missing approvals. The pack also includes the approval limits and the payment procedure. As a group, test the files against the procedure and produce: a test sheet in a spreadsheet recording, for each file, whether each control was met (approval within limits, three-way match, two signatures, correct coding) and any exceptions; a summary showing the exception rate for each control, calculated correctly; a two-page findings report with the likely cause of each weakness, its risk and the recommended action; and an action plan with owners and dates. Then hold a 15-minute role-played meeting with the 'finance manager' (played by the assessor or a member of another group) to present the findings and agree the actions, with minutes taken. Give each member a named role: audit lead (plans the testing and chairs the meeting), two testers (each tests half of the files), analyst (builds the summary and checks the rates), and report writer and minute-taker. In a group of four, the analyst also takes the minutes. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Pack of 40 made-up payment files from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software
photos: The files laid out and split between the testers
The test sheet on screen with exceptions marked
The findings report and action plan
The signed minutes of the meeting
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Tested each file accurately against the procedure
Identified likely causes, not only the errors
Recommended practical actions with owners and dates
Presented findings respectfully and factually in the meeting
Kept the files confidential and returned them complete
safety: Use only the made-up files and do not copy real organisations' documents
Keep the files and findings confidential to the group and the assessor
Report findings about processes, not personal blame, in the meeting
Share the workload fairly and take short breaks
